did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with a prophetic date associated with the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, but later the message is addressed to Zedekiah and the kings of the surrounding nations. Thus, the chapter places the prophecy within a broad political context.
Did you know? The Lord commands Jeremiah to make straps and yoke bars and put them on his neck. In this chapter, the yoke serves as a tangible symbol of political subjugation to the king of Babylon.
Did you know? Jeremiah is instructed to send the symbol of the yoke through messengers to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon, who had gathered in Jerusalem with Zedekiah king of Judah.

Did you know? The chapter’s justification for Babylon’s rule begins with the Lord’s declaration that he created the earth, humanity, and the animals, and therefore has the authority to give the lands to whomever he considers right.
Did you know? Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is called “my servant” in this chapter. According to the prophecy, the Lord gave the lands—and even the wild animals—into his hands to serve him.

Did you know? The chapter describes the continuation of Nebuchadnezzar’s rule by mentioning him, his son, and his grandson. After that, the time of his own land will come, and Babylon itself will be ruled by other nations and kings.

Did you know? Jeremiah warns the people not to listen to the prophets, diviners, dreamers, fortune-tellers, or sorcerers who promise that they will not have to serve the king of Babylon. The chapter presents their words as false prophecy.
Did you know? Jeremiah appeals to Zedekiah to place his neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him and his people, so that he may live rather than die by the sword, famine, and plague.

Did you know? The false prophets promised that the vessels of the Lord’s temple taken to Babylon would soon be returned, but Jeremiah rejects their promise. He even says that if they are true prophets, they should pray to prevent the vessels still remaining in Jerusalem from being taken away.

Did you know? According to the end of the chapter, the vessels still remaining in the Lord’s temple, the royal palace, and Jerusalem will also be brought to Babylon. But they will not remain there forever: they will stay there until the day of reckoning, and then they will be returned to their proper place.
